issues.description: The study plans to combine a nationally representative sample of 2,500 adults with an oversample of 1,500 sports bettors. Without applying survey weights or analyzing the groups separately, the pooled sample of 4,000 will no longer be nationally representative, artificially inflating the prevalence of gambling and potentially other behaviors, which biases the population-level estimates.
issues.quote: This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.description: The manuscript explicitly contradicts itself regarding who will complete the problematic use measures. In the Measures section, it states that only past-year users will complete them. In the Data Screening section, it states that all participants will complete them regardless of engagement. This fundamentally changes the sample size, variance, and zero-inflation of the dependent variables.
issues.quote: Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use." vs "we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample.
issues.location: Method - Measures / Data Screening and Inclusion Criteria

issues.description: The authors plan to average five NIDA-ASSIST items to create a problematic use score. However, three items use a 0-5 scale and two items use a 0, 3, 6 scale. Averaging these without prior standardization will disproportionately weight the items with the 0, 3, 6 scale, altering the psychometric properties of the measure.
issues.quote: Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest

issues.description: The text states that gambling frequency will be measured by taking an average across multiple gambling behaviors. However, the supplemental materials only provide a single item ('Gambled or placed bets at all') for gambling frequency.
issues.quote: To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken.

issues.description: There are multiple discrepancies between the scales described in the text and those in the supplemental materials. For example, the text describes the frequency scale as '0 (never) to 5' for substances but '1 (never) to 6' for pornography and gambling. The Brief Pornography Screen is described as a 'three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often)' in the text, but the supplement lists 'Never (0) | Occasionally (2) | Very Often (4)'.
issues.quote: scale of 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day)" vs "scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day)

issues.description: The authors state they will conduct 8 moderation analyses for 8 target behaviors. However, only 7 behaviors are listed in the manuscript (Alcohol, Tobacco/Nicotine, Cannabis, Prescription Drugs, Illicit Drugs, Pornography, Gambling). It is unclear what the 8th behavior or analysis is.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest

issues.description: The authors plan to conduct at least 7 (or 8) primary moderation analyses to test their hypotheses, but they do not mention any alpha level correction (e.g., Bonferroni, Holm) for these primary regression models, which inflates the family-wise error rate.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency

issues.description: For a Registered Report, analytic plans must be highly specific to prevent researcher degrees of freedom. Stating that supplemental analyses will be conducted 'as appropriate' if assumptions are violated is too vague. The specific non-parametric or robust statistical methods must be pre-registered.
issues.quote: in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate.

issues.description: The manuscript contains contradictory statements about the Smallest Effect Size of Interest (SESOI). It first states the SESOI is δ = .27, then immediately says it is set to β = .11 (and δ = |.11|). This inconsistency makes the primary equivalence bounds ambiguous.
issues.quote: with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .27... we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above (β=.11

issues.description: Table 2 provides the power to detect an effect (f2 = .015) significantly different from zero. However, the core hypotheses (2b and 3b) rely on equivalence testing. The authors do not report the statistical power to reject the null hypothesis of the equivalence test (i.e., power to detect that an effect falls within the equivalence bounds).
issues.quote: a series of sensitivity analyses to determine the likely power our final sample sizes would have to detect the effect size associated with our SESOI and equivalence region defined above, and a series of estimated achieved power based. The results are summarized in Table 2 below.

issues.description: The authors state that if they lack power, they will use an alternative equivalence region based on the lower bound of a previous study's CI (β = .23). An equivalence bound of β = .23 is very large; finding an effect within this bound does not mean the effect is 'practically zero,' but rather just smaller than a previously observed large effect. This misaligns with the hypothesis that the interaction will not predict symptoms.
issues.quote: we will test an alternative model where our equivalence region is defined by the lower bound of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate of moral incongruence in predicting self-reported addiction to pornography (β = .27, 95% CI [.23, .31]

issues.description: In the 'The Present Study' section, the authors define moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval and 'severity of consequences.' This contradicts their entire theoretical framework and the rest of the manuscript, which defines it as the interaction of moral disapproval and 'frequency of engaging in that behavior.'
issues.quote: Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action.

issues.description: Moral disapproval for using illicit drugs or misusing prescription drugs is likely to be extremely high for the vast majority of the population. This will result in severe ceiling effects and restricted variance for the moral disapproval moderator, which will artificially attenuate the interaction effect, potentially leading to a false negative that supports their hypothesis for artifactual reasons.
issues.quote: I believe that using prescription drugs for non-medical reasons is morally wrong

issues.description: The authors state they will not remove any responses for inattentive or careless responding because they rely entirely on YouGov's proprietary quality control. For a Registered Report, researchers should pre-specify their own objective data quality checks (e.g., attention check items, minimum completion time, straight-lining indices) rather than blindly trusting a panel provider.
issues.quote: we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding.
issues.location: Method - Data Screening and Inclusion Criteria

issues.description: The authors plan to code gender as a binary variable (1 = male, 0 = not-male). This approach lumps females and non-binary/other gender identities into a single category, which can confound the covariate. Non-binary participants should be handled explicitly (e.g., excluded if n is too small, or coded as a separate dummy variable).

The authors claim they anticipate no unplanned missingness. However, in a survey of 4,000 people, item non-response or dropouts are inevitable. A Registered Report must pre-specify exactly how missing data will be handled (e.g., listwise deletion, full information maximum likelihood, multiple imputation).
issues.quote: we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.
issues.location: Method - Data Screening and Inclusion Criteria

issues.description: The manuscript contradicts itself regarding how variables will be prepared for moderation analysis. In one paragraph, it states that predictors and moderators will be centered before calculating the interaction term. In the next paragraph, it states they will be entered in their raw form and their product computed.
issues.quote: focal predictors (behavioral frequency measures) and moderators (moral disapproval questions) will be centered and their interaction term calculated." vs "For moderation analyses, key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed.
